moments.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
moments.who: Adam Smith, Glasgow Professor of Moral Philosophy
moments.body: Before Wealth of Nations, Smith was a moral philosopher. The Theory of Moral Sentiments grounds ethics in 'sympathy' — our capacity to imagine others' situations. The 'impartial spectator' is the figure we internalise to judge ourselves.

quote.text: How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature which interest him in the fortune of others.

moments.takeaway: The 'Adam Smith problem' — apparent tension between TMS's sympathy and Wealth of Nations' self-interest — has been mostly resolved by reading them together. Smith never thought economics was separate from ethics.

moments.title: The Wealth of Nations
moments.body: Published 9 March 1776, the same year as American independence. Smith argues that division of labour drives productivity (the pin factory example), that markets coordinate via voluntary exchange, and that mercantilism (protecting domestic producers via tariffs) is a transfer to politically connected interests rather than a path to wealth.

quote.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.

moments.takeaway: Smith's argument against mercantilism is still alive in trade policy debates today. His positive case for markets is hedged by warnings about monopoly, collusion and the political power of merchants.

now.title: Reading Smith today
now.body: Emma Rothschild ('Economic Sentiments', 2001) and Amartya Sen have both argued Smith has been mis-claimed by 20th-century libertarians. The actual Smith supports a substantial role for state provision of education, public works and regulation of banking. He is also clear-eyed about colonial exploitation and slavery.
now.open_questions: How much should economics be a 'science' separated from moral philosophy? Smith would have said the question makes no sense. Modern welfare economics, behavioural economics and the post-2008 turn have partly re-merged what 20th-century neoclassicism separated.

items.reflection: Adam Smith was a moral philosopher who happened to write the foundational text of modern economics. Reading the Wealth of Nations without the Theory of Moral Sentiments is reading half the man.

moments.title: The Communist Manifesto
moments.body: Published in February 1848, weeks before revolutions broke out across Europe. The pamphlet is a sweeping historical argument: history is the history of class struggle, capitalism has revolutionised production but produces its own contradictions, the proletariat will eventually overthrow it.

quote.text: A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of communism.
quote.attrib: Manifesto of the Communist Party, opening line

moments.takeaway: The 1848 revolutions failed within months. Marx and Engels fled to England. The Manifesto's influence was limited at first; it became a foundational text only after Marx's death.

moments.title: Das Kapital, Volume I
moments.who: Marx, after 20 years of research in the British Museum
moments.body: Marx's major theoretical work analyses capitalist production. The labour theory of value (commodities have value proportional to socially necessary labour time), the theory of surplus value (workers produce more value than they receive in wages), and the tendency of the rate of profit to fall — all are developed here.
moments.takeaway: Volumes II and III were published posthumously by Engels (1885, 1894). Modern economists generally reject the labour theory of value in its classical form, but Marx's analysis of crisis, concentration and exploitation remains intellectually serious.

now.title: Marx after the Cold War
now.body: The collapse of state socialism in 1989-91 was widely read as Marx's refutation. But the 2008 financial crisis revived interest in Marxian analysis of debt, crisis and class. Thomas Piketty's 'Capital in the Twenty-First Century' (2013) — not Marxist but engaging similar questions about inheritance, wealth concentration and rentier capitalism — sold millions.
now.open_questions: Was Marx wrong about everything because the USSR collapsed? Most serious historians distinguish Marx's analytical work from later Marxist-Leninist political practice. The question of whether capitalism's contradictions still drive history is genuinely open.

items.reflection: Marx is more often invoked than read. The actual texts are dense, often empirical, and reward close reading regardless of where you stand politically.

moments.title: The Wall Street Crash
moments.who: Investors and the New York Stock Exchange
moments.body: On 24 October ('Black Thursday') and 29 October ('Black Tuesday') 1929, US stock prices crashed. The Dow lost almost 90% of its value by 1932. US unemployment hit 25%. The Great Depression spread globally. Classical economics, with its faith in self-correcting markets, had no convincing response.
moments.takeaway: The intellectual crisis was as severe as the economic one. The discipline needed a new framework.

moments.title: The General Theory
moments.body: Keynes's 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' argues that aggregate demand drives output, that economies can be stuck at high-unemployment equilibrium, and that government spending can shift them. The 'multiplier' makes fiscal policy potent. Saving is not automatically investment; liquidity preference matters.

quote.text: In the long run we are all dead.
quote.attrib: Keynes, A Tract on Monetary Reform, 1923

moments.takeaway: Keynes shifted economics from a primarily microeconomic, equilibrium-based discipline to one with a distinct macroeconomic theory of slumps and policy.

moments.title: Bretton Woods
moments.who: Keynes, Harry Dexter White, and delegates from 44 nations
moments.body: At Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, the postwar international monetary system is designed. The dollar is pegged to gold, other currencies to the dollar. The IMF and the World Bank are founded. Keynes's proposal for a global currency (the 'bancor') was rejected; White's dollar-centred system won.
moments.takeaway: Bretton Woods underpinned 25 years of postwar growth ('les trente glorieuses'). It collapsed in 1971 when Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility.

now.title: Keynes after Keynes
now.body: Monetarism (Friedman) and New Classical economics (Lucas) eclipsed Keynesianism from the late 1970s, partly in response to the failure of crude Keynesian models in the stagflation of the 1970s. The 2008 crisis brought a Keynesian revival — Paul Krugman, Olivier Blanchard, Mark Carney all explicitly invoked Keynes. Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) has roots in chartalist Keynesianism.
now.open_questions: Was the 2008-21 era proof Keynes was right, or did near-zero interest rates expose the limits of monetary policy and the need for new frameworks? The post-COVID inflation revived doubts about loose fiscal policy.

items.reflection: Keynes thought economics should serve civilisation, not constrain it. The 'Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren' (1930) essay imagined that by 2030 the economic problem would be solved and we'd worry about the use of leisure. It hasn't worked out that way — but the question is still live.

moments.title: Prospect Theory
moments.body: Kahneman and Tversky publish 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk' in Econometrica. The paper documents systematic departures from expected-utility theory: loss aversion, reference dependence, probability weighting. It is the founding text of behavioural economics.
moments.takeaway: Both authors were psychologists. The paper landing in an economics journal was itself a disciplinary event.

moments.title: Nudge
moments.body: Thaler and Sunstein's 'Nudge' popularises 'libertarian paternalism' — choice architecture that steers people toward better decisions without restricting freedom. Default enrollment in pension schemes, organ donation opt-out systems, school meal layouts. The UK government's Behavioural Insights Team ('Nudge Unit') is set up in 2010.
moments.takeaway: Behavioural economics moved from journal articles to policy practice within a decade.

moments.title: Nobel prizes confirm the shift
moments.body: Kahneman shares the 2002 Nobel with Vernon Smith. Thaler wins in 2017. Esther Duflo, Abhijit Banerjee and Michael Kremer (2019) win for randomised controlled trials in development — methodologically related, applying experimental rigour to policy.
moments.takeaway: By the 2010s, the rational-agent model of textbook microeconomics is widely treated as a useful approximation rather than a description.

now.title: Behavioural economics goes mainstream
now.body: Major employers, insurers, governments now use behavioural insights routinely. Critics (notably Gerd Gigerenzer) argue that some 'biases' are actually adaptive heuristics in real-world environments, and that the focus on individual cognition lets institutions off the hook. The replication crisis in psychology (2011 onwards) has forced behavioural economics to re-examine some of its standard findings.
now.open_questions: Should governments nudge? Critics across the political spectrum worry about manipulation. Defenders point out that choice architecture exists whether or not it's designed deliberately, so designing it deliberately is at least transparent.

items.reflection: Behavioural economics is one of the rare cases where a research programme overturned a dominant theoretical assumption (the rational agent) and reshaped policy practice in a generation.

moments.title: Principles of Political Economy and Taxation
moments.body: Ricardo, a successful stockbroker turned MP, publishes his Principles. Chapter 7 introduces the theory of comparative advantage using the famous Portugal-England, wine-and-cloth example. Even if one country can produce both goods more efficiently in absolute terms, both countries gain from specialisation according to relative opportunity costs.

quote.text: Under a system of perfectly free commerce, each country naturally devotes its capital and labour to such employments as are most beneficial to each.
quote.attrib: Ricardo, Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, 1817

moments.takeaway: A non-intuitive theoretical result became one of the most powerful arguments for free trade — and remains so 200 years later.

moments.title: Repeal of the Corn Laws
moments.body: The UK repeals the Corn Laws, removing tariffs on imported grain. The decision splits the Conservative Party. Free trade ideology, drawing on Smith and Ricardo, becomes dominant UK economic policy through the 19th century.
moments.takeaway: Economic ideas can drive political realignment when interests align with intellectual frameworks.

now.title: Comparative advantage today
now.body: The basic logic remains valid; modern trade theory (Krugman 1991 on new trade theory, Eaton-Kortum on geography of trade, Melitz on heterogeneous firms) extends it. The political economy of trade — winners and losers within countries — has become more salient as adjustment costs of liberalisation have proven larger than originally assumed.
now.open_questions: How should trade policy account for distributional consequences without abandoning the aggregate gains?

items.reflection: Ricardo's theory is one of the few results in social science that's both non-obvious and broadly correct. Its policy implications are politically harder than its analytics.

moments.title: The marginalist revolution
moments.who: William Stanley Jevons (UK), Carl Menger (Austria), Léon Walras (Switzerland)
moments.body: Three economists independently publish works centred on marginal analysis: Jevons's Theory of Political Economy, Menger's Grundsätze, and shortly after Walras's Éléments d'économie politique pure (1874). The classical labour theory of value is replaced by subjective utility maximisation at the margin.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical reframing emerged in three places at once — a sign the ideas were intellectually ripe.

moments.title: Marshall's Principles of Economics
moments.body: Marshall synthesises marginalism with classical concerns into a comprehensive textbook. The supply-and-demand cross diagram, consumer surplus, elasticity, the long-run/short-run distinction — all become standard. Marshall's textbook dominates teaching for decades.
moments.takeaway: Synthesis and pedagogical reach can matter as much as theoretical originality in establishing a paradigm.

now.title: Neoclassical economics
now.body: Marginalist analysis remains the backbone of microeconomics. General equilibrium (Arrow-Debreu 1954) extended Walras's approach. The 20th century added game theory, mechanism design and behavioural extensions. Critics argue marginalism's focus on equilibrium understates power, distribution and instability.
now.open_questions: Can equilibrium-based models handle structural change, crisis and innovation, or do they need fundamental rethinking?

items.reflection: The marginalist revolution is the moment economics became something a mathematics graduate could pursue without becoming a moral philosopher first. The gains in precision came with losses of breadth that economics has been negotiating since.

moments.title: Bretton Woods Conference
moments.who: Delegates from 44 nations; Keynes (UK) and White (US) led negotiations
moments.body: From 1-22 July 1944 at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, delegates from 44 nations design the postwar international monetary system. The US dollar is pegged to gold ($35/oz); other currencies are pegged to the dollar. The IMF and the IBRD (later World Bank) are founded. Keynes's proposed global currency (the bancor) is rejected in favour of White's dollar-centred design.
moments.takeaway: International monetary architecture was deliberately designed by negotiation, not evolved. The choices made shaped 25 years of postwar economic order.

moments.title: The end of Bretton Woods
moments.body: On 15 August 1971 Nixon ends dollar-gold convertibility, devalues the dollar and imposes a 90-day wage-price freeze. The Smithsonian Agreement (December) attempts to salvage fixed parities; it fails by 1973. Major currencies float against each other from 1973.
moments.takeaway: The Triffin dilemma — that the US could not indefinitely supply world reserves while maintaining gold convertibility — eventually forced the collapse.

now.title: After Bretton Woods
now.body: Floating exchange rates have prevailed since 1973 for major currencies, with managed floats and currency pegs for many others. The IMF's role evolved from defending parities to crisis lending. The dollar's reserve role persists despite repeated forecasts of decline. Discussions of alternatives (SDRs, BRICS currency, digital currencies) recur without yet displacing the dollar.
now.open_questions: What replaces a system whose foundational arrangement (gold convertibility) has been gone for half a century but whose institutions persist?

items.reflection: The Bretton Woods system was a deliberate political-economic design. Its successor is more an accumulated set of compromises than a designed system, with corresponding fragilities.

moments.title: A Monetary History of the United States
moments.body: Friedman and Schwartz argue from US data that the Great Depression was made far worse by the Federal Reserve's failure to prevent monetary contraction. The book reframes monetary policy as crucial — a direct challenge to the Keynesian consensus.
moments.takeaway: Re-analysis of historical data can challenge a prevailing macroeconomic interpretation.

moments.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
moments.body: Friedman argues there is no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the 'natural rate' of unemployment. Edmund Phelps had reached similar conclusions independently. The 1970s stagflation provides empirical support.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical prediction precedes its empirical confirmation by years; both then reshape policy.

moments.title: Volcker's disinflation
moments.body: Volcker, appointed Fed chair in 1979, raises interest rates dramatically (Fed Funds rate peaks at 19% in 1981) to break inflation. US unemployment peaks at 10.8% in 1982. Inflation falls from 13.5% in 1980 to 3.2% by 1983. The disinflation is painful but lasting.
moments.takeaway: Severe monetary tightening can break inflation — at substantial short-run cost. The Volcker disinflation reshaped central bank credibility.

now.title: After monetarism
now.body: Strict monetarism (control of monetary aggregates) was abandoned by most central banks in the 1990s as money-velocity relationships became unstable. Inflation targeting (NZ 1989, UK 1992, Sweden 1993) became the new orthodoxy. Friedman's broader insight — that monetary policy matters and central bank credibility is foundational — remains influential.
now.open_questions: How should central banks operate in a world of repeatedly hitting the zero lower bound? The post-2008 toolkit (QE, forward guidance) is partly an answer.

items.reflection: Friedman did to mid-century Keynesianism what Keynes had done to pre-1936 orthodoxy. The intellectual cycle continued after 2008 with the partial Keynesian revival.

moments.title: Thatcher elected
moments.body: Thatcher's government implements monetarist policy (Medium Term Financial Strategy), privatisation (BT 1984, British Gas 1986, water 1989, electricity 1990), trade union reform and income tax cuts. UK unemployment peaks above 3 million by 1984.
moments.takeaway: A sustained policy programme over 11 years transformed the UK economic model — with substantial regional and distributional consequences.

moments.title: Reagan elected, Volcker continues
moments.body: Reagan's administration combines monetary tightening (Volcker, continued from Carter), tax cuts (1981 Economic Recovery Tax Act, 1986 Tax Reform Act) and deregulation. Federal deficit widens substantially.
moments.takeaway: 'Reaganomics' combined supply-side, monetarist and small-government ideas — and ran sustained deficits despite small-government rhetoric.

moments.title: Big Bang
moments.body: On 27 October 1986, deregulation of the London Stock Exchange ends fixed commissions and the separation of jobbers and brokers, allowing foreign ownership of UK firms. London's role as global financial centre is consolidated.
moments.takeaway: Financial deregulation reshaped the UK economy's composition (more services, financial services especially) for decades.

now.title: Legacies of the 1980s
now.body: Privatisation, financial deregulation, tax structures, and weakened collective bargaining all persist as central features of the UK and US economies. The 2008 crisis prompted partial reversal in financial regulation; broader Thatcher/Reagan era settlements have endured. Recent decades have seen growing concentration, rising inequality, and stagnant median wages in both countries — all subject to ongoing debate about causes.
now.open_questions: Was the 1980s reform package a one-time correction of postwar excesses or a structural shift whose costs are now visible? Both interpretations have proponents.

items.reflection: The 1980s reshaped what was politically possible across the political spectrum. The next decade's New Labour and New Democrat parties accepted much of the framework. The aftermath of 2008 reopened debates the 1980s seemed to have settled.

moments.title: Maastricht Treaty
moments.body: The Treaty on European Union (signed February 1992) sets out the convergence criteria for joining the euro: inflation, deficit, debt, exchange rate stability and long-term interest rates. The UK and Denmark secure opt-outs.
moments.takeaway: Monetary union was designed as a multi-decade institutional project, not an organic outcome.

moments.title: Euro launched
moments.body: On 1 January 1999 the euro is launched as an accounting currency; exchange rates are irrevocably fixed. Physical notes and coins enter circulation in 2002. 12 countries initially adopt; by 2024, 20 EU members use the euro.
moments.takeaway: A monetary union without fiscal or banking union proceeded despite warnings — including from many economists — about its sustainability.

moments.title: Eurozone debt crisis
moments.body: Sovereign debt crises hit eurozone periphery. Greece receives bailouts (2010, 2012, 2015); Ireland and Portugal also; Spain restructures its banks. Mario Draghi's July 2012 'whatever it takes' speech stabilises markets. Outright Monetary Transactions and later QE follow.
moments.takeaway: Monetary union faced the test of asymmetric shocks without fiscal transfers. The system survived but at significant cost to peripheral economies.

now.title: Eurozone today
now.body: Banking union is partial (single supervision yes, deposit insurance no). Fiscal union remains limited; the 2020 Next Generation EU recovery fund (€750bn) marked unprecedented common borrowing. The euro is the second most-used reserve currency. Internal imbalances (current accounts, productivity divergence) persist.
now.open_questions: Can a monetary union without full fiscal union manage the next major crisis? The institutional architecture has been incrementally extended but its core design tension remains.

items.reflection: Optimum currency area theory (Mundell 1961) provided clear conditions for monetary union viability. The eurozone met few of them in 1999 — and political commitment, not economic optimality, drove the project.

moments.title: Subprime troubles
moments.who: US mortgage markets, Bear Stearns, BNP Paribas, Northern Rock
moments.body: US subprime mortgage defaults rise; mortgage-backed securities lose value. BNP Paribas freezes funds in August. Northern Rock experiences first UK bank run since 1866 (September), is nationalised February 2008.
moments.takeaway: Wholesale funding markets froze months before the most visible failures.

moments.title: Lehman, then the panic
moments.body: Lehman Brothers files for Chapter 11 on 15 September 2008 — the largest US bankruptcy ever. AIG, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac all require federal rescue. UK government recapitalises RBS and Lloyds. TARP ($700bn) passes 3 October. Coordinated central bank rate cuts 8 October.
moments.takeaway: A coordinated global response prevented a deeper depression but at the cost of large public debt expansion and political backlash.

moments.title: Recession and reform
moments.body: Global GDP contracts in 2009 (the first global contraction since the 1930s by some measures). Major reform packages: Dodd-Frank Act (US 2010), Vickers Commission (UK 2011, leading to ring-fencing 2019), Basel III (2010-13). Central bank balance sheets expand dramatically.
moments.takeaway: Crisis triggered the largest regulatory overhaul since the 1930s, and macroeconomic policy entered an unconventional decade.

now.title: After 2008
now.body: Macroprudential frameworks have grown across countries. Stress tests are routine. Risk has migrated to less-regulated 'shadow' lending. The political fallout — populism, inequality salience, distrust of expertise — has shaped politics across democracies. Subsequent crises (eurozone, 2020 pandemic, 2023 SVB/Credit Suisse) have tested but not broken the post-2008 framework.
now.open_questions: Have the reforms made the system fundamentally safer, or simply moved risk to less-monitored corners?

items.reflection: The 2008 crisis broke the Great Moderation, the consensus around financial deregulation, and the academic confidence in DSGE models without banking. Its consequences still shape policy a generation later.

moments.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
moments.body: Malthus argues population grows geometrically while subsistence grows arithmetically, producing recurrent checks through famine, war and disease.
moments.takeaway: Population pressure provides a pessimistic frame for classical economics.

moments.title: Second edition
moments.body: Malthus expands his argument and adds 'moral restraint' as a preventive check, softening the original pessimism.
moments.takeaway: Theorists revise hard predictions under counterargument.

moments.title: The Population Bomb
moments.body: Ehrlich revives Malthusian alarm about population growth, predicting mass famine. Predictions are largely falsified by the Green Revolution.
moments.takeaway: Malthusian predictions recur and are repeatedly tested by technology.

now.title: Malthus after the Green Revolution
now.body: Climate change, biodiversity loss and water stress have revived modified Malthusian framings, alongside critiques rooted in Sen's entitlement theory of famine.
now.open_questions: Are planetary boundaries a new Malthusian constraint, or do they require a different framework?

items.reflection: Malthus was a clergyman and demographer as well as an economist; the gloom of his essay shaped Carlyle's 'dismal science' label.

moments.title: Essay on Profits
moments.body: Ricardo argues against the Corn Laws, foreshadowing his theory of rent and free trade.
moments.takeaway: Policy questions drove classical theory development.

moments.title: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation
moments.body: Ricardo formalises comparative advantage with the famous Portugal-England wine-and-cloth example.
moments.takeaway: Even an absolutely less efficient country gains from trade.

moments.title: Repeal of the Corn Laws
moments.body: Britain repeals the Corn Laws under Robert Peel, marking a victory for free-trade arguments influenced by Ricardo.
moments.takeaway: Theory can shape national policy a generation after publication.

now.title: Comparative advantage today
now.body: Modern trade theory (Krugman, Melitz) supplements Ricardo with increasing returns, monopolistic competition and firm heterogeneity.
now.open_questions: How should comparative advantage be taught alongside concerns about deindustrialisation and supply chain vulnerability?

items.reflection: Ricardo, a wealthy stockbroker turned MP, helped invent economics as a profession in his short life.

moments.title: Principles of Political Economy
moments.body: Mill's text dominates economics teaching for half a century, distinguishing laws of production (technical) from laws of distribution (political).
moments.takeaway: Distinguishing production and distribution opened space for redistributive policy.

moments.title: On Liberty
moments.body: Mill's defence of individual liberty and the harm principle shapes liberal economics' commitment to personal autonomy.
moments.takeaway: Liberal political philosophy underpinned classical economics.

moments.title: The Subjection of Women
moments.body: Mill argues that women's exclusion from economic and political life is one of the chief obstacles to human progress.
moments.takeaway: Classical economists could be radical on gender.

now.title: Mill in modern economics
now.body: Mill's distinction between production and distribution underpins welfare economics. His advocacy for cooperatives and worker democracy remains influential.
now.open_questions: Should modern economics still teach Mill's distinction or treat distribution as endogenous to production?

items.reflection: Mill was educated at home by his father from age three; his Autobiography records both the brilliance and the cost of that education.

moments.title: The Theory of Political Economy
moments.body: Jevons grounds value in marginal utility, mathematicising the diminishing satisfaction of additional units.
moments.takeaway: Marginal analysis replaces labour theories of value.

moments.title: Principles of Economics
moments.body: Menger independently develops marginal utility, founding the Austrian school with its emphasis on subjective value and time.
moments.takeaway: Independent discovery suggests an idea whose time has come.

moments.title: Elements of Pure Economics
moments.body: Walras formalises general equilibrium across multiple markets, foreshadowing 20th-century mathematical economics.
moments.takeaway: Walras's framework underpinned much later neoclassical economics.

now.title: The marginalist legacy
now.body: Marginal analysis remains foundational to mainstream microeconomics. Austrian, mathematical and behavioural traditions all trace lineages to the 1870s.
now.open_questions: How do behavioural and ecological findings reshape the assumption of utility maximisation?

items.reflection: Three nearly simultaneous discoveries gave neoclassical economics its conceptual core.

moments.title: Principles of Economics
moments.body: Marshall's textbook synthesises classical and marginalist thinking. The supply-and-demand diagram (the 'scissors') becomes the discipline's visual icon.

quote.text: We might as reasonably dispute whether it is the upper or the under blade of a pair of scissors that cuts a piece of paper.

moments.takeaway: Diagrams shape how a discipline thinks.

moments.title: Economics tripos established
moments.body: Marshall lobbies for and obtains a separate economics tripos, separating the discipline from moral sciences.
moments.takeaway: Disciplinary autonomy required institutional change.

moments.title: Industry and Trade
moments.body: Marshall's late work analyses industrial districts, foreshadowing modern cluster theory.
moments.takeaway: Even synthesisers contribute distinct empirical work.

now.title: Marshall in modern economics
now.body: Industrial districts, economic geography and Cambridge controversies all trace lineages to Marshall.
now.open_questions: How does the partial-equilibrium tradition of Marshall coexist with computable general equilibrium models today?

items.reflection: Marshall said high theory should be 'translated into English' and burned the equations from his textbook footnotes.

moments.title: Mr Keynes and the Classics
moments.body: Hicks's Econometrica paper translates Keynes's General Theory into the IS-LM diagram that dominates macroeconomics teaching for fifty years.
moments.takeaway: An influential simplification can outlast the original text.

moments.title: Value and Capital
moments.body: Hicks's book formalises general equilibrium and consumer theory in a way that shapes postwar microeconomics.
moments.takeaway: Hicks contributed across micro and macro foundations.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Hicks and Arrow share the Nobel Prize for general equilibrium theory.
moments.takeaway: General equilibrium became canonical.

now.title: Beyond IS-LM
now.body: Modern macro uses dynamic stochastic general equilibrium and heterogeneous-agent models; IS-LM remains a teaching tool.
now.open_questions: Do recent zero-lower-bound experiences require new diagrammatic tools?

items.reflection: Hicks later expressed doubts about how IS-LM had been used, while accepting its pedagogical power.

moments.title: The Economics of Welfare
moments.body: Pigou formalises externalities and proposes taxes and subsidies to align private and social costs.
moments.takeaway: Welfare economics provided a justification for state intervention.

moments.title: The Problem of Social Cost
moments.body: Coase argues that when transaction costs are low, private bargaining can resolve externalities without state intervention.
moments.takeaway: Property rights and bargaining can substitute for Pigovian taxes.

moments.title: Coase Nobel Prize
moments.body: Coase receives the Nobel for transaction costs and property rights analysis.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical clarification can reorient a field.

now.title: Externalities and climate
now.body: Carbon taxes (Pigovian) and emissions trading (Coasian) are the two main policy instruments for climate change.
now.open_questions: Why have carbon prices remained below most economist estimates of the social cost of carbon?

items.reflection: The Pigou-Coase debate structures modern environmental economics.

moments.title: The Calculus of Consent
moments.body: Buchanan and Tullock apply economic analysis to political decision-making, founding public choice economics.
moments.takeaway: Politicians and voters can be analysed as rational actors.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Buchanan receives the Nobel for public choice theory.
moments.takeaway: Public choice was recognised as a distinct subfield.

moments.title: Public choice in practice
moments.body: Public choice frameworks inform OECD analysis of regulatory capture, lobbying and fiscal rules.
moments.takeaway: Theory enters governance practice.

now.title: Government failure
now.body: Public choice frames remain central to libertarian critique of state action. Critics (MacLean) note its links to anti-democratic strands of US politics.
now.open_questions: How should public choice be balanced with renewed attention to market failure in climate and inequality?

items.reflection: Buchanan's Virginia school built a distinct institutional and political base for public choice.

moments.title: The Market for Lemons
moments.body: Akerlof shows that asymmetric information about quality can cause markets to unravel, using used cars as the example.
moments.takeaway: Information asymmetries are a major source of market failure.

moments.title: Job Market Signaling
moments.body: Spence shows education can serve as a costly signal in labour markets even when it does not raise productivity.
moments.takeaway: Signalling can sustain markets in the presence of asymmetry.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: The Nobel Prize is awarded for the analysis of markets with asymmetric information.
moments.takeaway: Information economics is recognised as foundational.

now.title: Information asymmetries online
now.body: Online reviews, ratings and algorithmic intermediation are analysed through Akerlof's framework.
now.open_questions: Do platform reputation systems solve or merely shift asymmetric-information problems?

items.reflection: Akerlof's paper was famously rejected by multiple journals before publication.

moments.title: Judgement under Uncertainty
moments.body: Their Science paper catalogues heuristics that systematically violate rational-choice assumptions.
moments.takeaway: Psychology can supply empirical micro-foundations.

moments.title: Prospect Theory
moments.body: Their Econometrica paper introduces an empirical theory of choice under risk featuring loss aversion and probability weighting.
moments.takeaway: Descriptive and normative theories of choice diverge measurably.

moments.title: Kahneman Nobel Prize
moments.body: Kahneman receives the Nobel for prospect theory; Tversky had died in 1996.
moments.takeaway: Behavioural economics enters the discipline's centre.

now.title: Behavioural economics today
now.body: Behavioural insights teams operate in many governments; the field has weathered a partial replication crisis.
now.open_questions: How robust are key behavioural effects under preregistration?

items.reflection: Two psychologists transformed economics' descriptive foundations.

moments.title: Toward a Positive Theory of Consumer Choice
moments.body: Thaler's paper introduces the endowment effect and other anomalies into economics.
moments.takeaway: Anomalies become subjects of study, not exceptions.

moments.title: Nudge
moments.body: Their book argues for 'libertarian paternalism' through default settings in pensions, organ donation and other domains.
moments.takeaway: Default settings have outsized effects on choices.

moments.title: Thaler Nobel Prize
moments.body: Thaler receives the Nobel for incorporating behavioural insights into economic analysis.
moments.takeaway: Behavioural economics is now mainstream.

now.title: Nudge in policy
now.body: UK Behavioural Insights Team and similar units operate globally. Effects size and ethics of nudge are now contested.
now.open_questions: Where is the line between nudging and manipulation in digital choice architectures?

items.reflection: Thaler made decision anomalies respectable in a discipline that long dismissed them.

moments.title: Poverty and Famines
moments.body: Sen's analysis of the 1943 Bengal famine and others argues famines reflect entitlement failures rather than absolute food shortage.
moments.takeaway: Famine is about access, not just availability.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Sen receives the Nobel for contributions to welfare economics.
moments.takeaway: Welfare economics gains a development-focused champion.

moments.title: Development as Freedom
moments.body: Sen articulates the capabilities approach: development as the expansion of substantive freedoms.
moments.takeaway: Income is one of many capabilities people have reason to value.

now.title: Capabilities in policy
now.body: Sen and Martha Nussbaum's framework underpins the UNDP Human Development Index and broader well-being metrics.
now.open_questions: How should capabilities be measured and aggregated in policy?

items.reflection: Sen has worked across economics, philosophy and development for sixty years.

moments.title: The Stages of Economic Growth
moments.body: Rostow proposes five stages of economic growth from traditional society to age of high mass consumption.
moments.takeaway: Modernisation theory framed Cold War development policy.

moments.title: Dependency theory critique
moments.body: Frank argues developing countries are not 'undeveloped' but 'under-developed' through their integration with the global economy.
moments.takeaway: Dependency theory challenged modernisation.

moments.title: World-Systems Analysis
moments.body: Wallerstein's framework analyses core, semi-periphery and periphery in a single capitalist world-economy.
moments.takeaway: Global capitalism produces structured inequalities.

now.title: Development theory today
now.body: Rostow's stages are largely abandoned; debates centre on industrial policy, institutions and the middle-income trap.
now.open_questions: Can late developers replicate the East Asian growth model in the era of climate constraints?

items.reflection: Rostow's subtitle was 'A Non-Communist Manifesto'; development theory was Cold War politics by other means.

moments.title: Colonial Origins of Comparative Development
moments.body: Their AER paper uses settler mortality as an instrument to identify long-run institutional effects on development.
moments.takeaway: Historical instruments can identify causal long-run effects.

moments.title: Why Nations Fail
moments.body: Their book argues inclusive vs extractive institutions explain why some nations grow and others stagnate.
moments.takeaway: Institutions are causal, not just correlated with growth.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: The Nobel is awarded for research on how institutions are formed and affect prosperity.
moments.takeaway: Institutional economics is recognised at the highest level.

now.title: Institutions and growth
now.body: Institutional analysis is central to development economics, alongside critiques pointing to colonial legacies, geography and culture.
now.open_questions: How can extractive institutions be reformed without revolution?

items.reflection: Acemoglu and Robinson's project rebuilt institutional economics as a quantitative field.

moments.title: Tulip mania peaks
moments.body: Speculation in tulip-bulb futures peaks in winter 1636-37. Bulbs trade for the price of houses.
moments.takeaway: Asset bubbles predate modern financial markets.

moments.title: Tulip crash
moments.body: Prices collapse in February 1637. Contemporary economic impact is now thought to have been smaller than later legend suggests.
moments.takeaway: Iconic crises can be partly mythologised.

moments.title: Mackay's Extraordinary Popular Delusions
moments.body: Mackay's book canonises tulip mania, the South Sea Bubble and the Mississippi Scheme for Victorian readers.
moments.takeaway: Financial history depends on the narratives that survive.

now.title: Bubbles in modern markets
now.body: Dot-com (2000), housing (2008) and crypto (2022) are analysed against the tulip template.
now.open_questions: Are some bubbles socially productive by funding speculative investment?

items.reflection: Tulip mania is more cautionary tale than reliable economic case study.

moments.title: South Sea Company founded
moments.body: The company is established to consolidate British government debt and trade in the South Atlantic.
moments.takeaway: Public debt and joint-stock speculation became intertwined.

moments.title: Bubble peak and crash
moments.body: South Sea shares rise from around 100 to 1,000 pounds and collapse to 150 by year end. Isaac Newton loses about 20,000 pounds.
moments.takeaway: Even brilliant individuals are not immune to bubbles.

moments.title: Bubble Act
moments.body: The Bubble Act restricts joint-stock company formation, slowing British corporate development for a century.
moments.takeaway: Crisis legislation can have long-run effects.

now.title: From South Sea to today
now.body: Modern financial regulation traces lineages to crisis-driven legislation including the Bubble Act, Glass-Steagall and Dodd-Frank.
now.open_questions: Does crisis-driven regulation systematically over- or under-shoot?

items.reflection: Newton reportedly said he could calculate the motions of the planets but not the madness of men.

moments.title: Black Thursday and Tuesday
moments.body: On 24 and 29 October 1929 US stock prices crash. The Dow loses nearly 90% of value by 1932.
moments.takeaway: A market crash triggered a decade-long depression.

moments.title: Glass-Steagall Act
moments.body: Glass-Steagall separates commercial from investment banking and establishes federal deposit insurance.
moments.takeaway: Banking reform followed financial collapse.

moments.title: A Monetary History of the United States
moments.body: Friedman and Schwartz argue the Great Depression was deepened by Federal Reserve inaction.
moments.takeaway: Monetary policy responses became a focus of historical analysis.

now.title: 1929 as cautionary template
now.body: Bernanke's response to 2008 was explicitly informed by the Friedman-Schwartz reading of 1929.
now.open_questions: How should monetary policy respond to bubbles ex ante rather than ex post?

items.reflection: The Great Depression remains the defining macroeconomic event for the discipline.

moments.title: Nixon ends dollar-gold convertibility
moments.body: Nixon's Sunday-evening 15 August announcement ends dollar-gold convertibility, effectively ending the Bretton Woods system.
moments.takeaway: Fixed exchange rates were abandoned by their hegemonic anchor.

moments.title: Generalised floating
moments.body: Major currencies move to floating exchange rates. Oil shocks the same year amplify the transition.
moments.takeaway: Floating rates became the new normal.

moments.title: Plaza Accord
moments.body: Coordinated G5 intervention depreciates the dollar. The accord demonstrates managed flexibility within a floating regime.
moments.takeaway: Floating rates allow coordinated intervention.

now.title: Currency regimes today
now.body: Mix of floating, pegged and currency-board regimes. Reserve currency status remains concentrated in dollar.
now.open_questions: Will Chinese yuan or digital currencies displace dollar dominance?

items.reflection: The collapse of Bretton Woods reshaped international macroeconomics and monetary theory.

moments.title: Black Monday
moments.body: On 19 October 1987 the Dow falls 22.6% in a single day, the largest one-day decline in history.
moments.takeaway: Programme trading and portfolio insurance amplified the crash.

moments.title: Brady Commission Report
moments.body: The report identifies portfolio insurance and index-arbitrage trading as crash amplifiers.
moments.takeaway: Financial innovation can create new fragilities.

moments.title: Circuit breakers introduced
moments.body: Circuit breakers pause trading after sharp declines, designed to interrupt panic cascades.
moments.takeaway: Market infrastructure can be redesigned after crises.

now.title: Flash crashes today
now.body: High-frequency trading has produced new flash-crash events, including the 2010 flash crash.
now.open_questions: Can regulation keep pace with algorithmic market microstructure?

items.reflection: Black Monday came without an obvious macroeconomic trigger, raising questions about market stability.

moments.title: Thai baht devalued
moments.body: Thailand abandons its dollar peg in July 1997. Currency speculation rapidly spreads to Indonesia, South Korea and the Philippines.
moments.takeaway: Currency crises can spread regionally.

moments.title: IMF interventions
moments.body: IMF bailouts impose austerity conditions that deepen recessions and trigger backlash.
moments.takeaway: Crisis lending carries political costs.

moments.title: Stiglitz dissent
moments.body: Stiglitz, then World Bank chief economist, publicly criticises IMF's response, leading to his departure.
moments.takeaway: Internal dissent shaped public debate over crisis response.

now.title: After Asia
now.body: East Asian economies built large foreign-exchange reserves after 1997. Reserve accumulation contributed to global imbalances pre-2008.
now.open_questions: How does the 1997 legacy shape Asian responses to current global financial stress?

items.reflection: Asia 1997 turned the IMF's reputation in much of the Global South.

moments.title: Greek debt revealed
moments.body: Greece reveals its deficit is far higher than reported, triggering sovereign-debt concerns across the eurozone periphery.
moments.takeaway: Statistical revisions can trigger crises.

moments.title: First Greek bailout
moments.body: The troika provides 110 billion euros in loans conditional on austerity measures.
moments.takeaway: Monetary union without fiscal union created governance gaps.

moments.title: Draghi's whatever it takes
moments.body: Draghi's London speech commits the ECB to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro, halting bond-market panic.

quote.text: Within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.

moments.takeaway: Central-bank communication can stabilise markets.

now.title: Eurozone reform
now.body: Banking union, ESM and pandemic-era NextGenerationEU funds extend eurozone fiscal capacity. Structural issues remain.
now.open_questions: Can the eurozone respond to climate transition costs without further integration?

items.reflection: The eurozone crisis showed how monetary union without fiscal union magnifies asymmetric shocks.

moments.title: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
moments.who: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern
moments.body: Their book founds game theory as a formal discipline, with minimax for zero-sum two-player games.
moments.takeaway: Strategic interaction became formally analysable.

moments.title: Nash equilibrium
moments.body: Nash's PhD thesis extends game theory to non-cooperative games with multiple players, defining the equilibrium concept that bears his name.
moments.takeaway: Nash equilibrium became the central solution concept.

moments.title: The Strategy of Conflict
moments.body: Schelling's book applies game theory to deterrence and nuclear strategy, introducing focal points and commitment devices.
moments.takeaway: Game theory shaped Cold War strategic thinking.

now.title: Game theory across fields
now.body: Auction design, market design and online platform economics all use modern game theory; Roth and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel for market design.
now.open_questions: How do behavioural and bounded-rationality refinements reshape applied game theory?

items.reflection: Game theory united economics, mathematics and Cold War strategy in mid-20th-century Princeton.

moments.title: Increasing Returns and Trade
moments.body: Krugman's paper explains how similar countries can trade similar goods through increasing returns and product differentiation.
moments.takeaway: Intra-industry trade required new theory.

moments.title: Geography and Trade
moments.body: Krugman's lectures launch new economic geography, modelling agglomeration in space.
moments.takeaway: Where economic activity locates became theoretically tractable.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Krugman receives the Nobel for the analysis of trade patterns and location of economic activity.
moments.takeaway: New trade theory entered the canon.

now.title: Trade and place today
now.body: Industrial policy revival, supply chain reshuffling and digital trade extend new trade and new economic geography research.
now.open_questions: How do remote work and digital services reshape the geography of agglomeration?

items.reflection: Krugman became a New York Times columnist after his Nobel, blending academic and public roles.

moments.title: Equilibrium in Competitive Insurance Markets
moments.body: Their paper analyses screening and self-selection in insurance markets with asymmetric information.
moments.takeaway: Asymmetric information complicates competitive equilibrium.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Stiglitz shares the Nobel for analysis of markets with asymmetric information.
moments.takeaway: Information economics is recognised.

moments.title: Globalization and Its Discontents
moments.body: Stiglitz's public-facing book criticises IMF, World Bank and US Treasury policies in developing countries.
moments.takeaway: Academic insider became outside critic.

now.title: Stiglitz on inequality
now.body: Stiglitz's later work on inequality, climate and corporate power continues his public-intellectual role.
now.open_questions: How should information-economics insights shape platform regulation?

items.reflection: Stiglitz combined frontier theoretical contributions with high-profile policy criticism.

moments.title: Volcker appointed Fed chair
moments.body: Paul Volcker becomes Federal Reserve chair as US inflation runs above 11%.
moments.takeaway: Inflation control required a credible institutional commitment.

moments.title: Fed funds rate at 20%
moments.body: Volcker's Fed raises rates to almost 20%, triggering a deep recession but breaking inflation.
moments.takeaway: Monetary policy could impose major real costs to credibility.

moments.title: Inflation falls below 4%
moments.body: US inflation falls below 4% by 1983. Unemployment peaked above 10% during the disinflation.
moments.takeaway: Disinflation succeeded but at substantial cost.

now.title: Volcker's shadow
now.body: Central bankers facing post-2021 inflation invoked the Volcker era and the lesson of letting expectations slip.
now.open_questions: Could a Volcker-style shock be politically tolerated in modern democracies?

items.reflection: Volcker's shock therapy reset macroeconomic expectations for a generation.

moments.title: Bank of England founded
moments.body: The Bank is founded to fund William III's war with France in exchange for the right to issue banknotes.
moments.takeaway: Public finance and central banking were intertwined from the start.

moments.title: Bank Charter Act
moments.body: The Act separates banking and issue departments and constrains note issue, foreshadowing modern central-bank governance.
moments.takeaway: Note issuance discipline shaped monetary architecture.

moments.title: Bank independence
moments.body: The Bank of England gains operational independence to set interest rates, mirroring the Fed and Bundesbank.
moments.takeaway: Central-bank independence became a global standard.

now.title: Central banking after 2008
now.body: Quantitative easing, forward guidance and macroprudential tools have expanded central-bank toolkits since 2008.
now.open_questions: Should central banks have explicit climate or distributional mandates?

items.reflection: The Bank of England is now the world's oldest continuously operating central bank.

moments.title: Panic of 1907
moments.body: JP Morgan personally organises private liquidity support to stop the panic, exposing the absence of a US central bank.
moments.takeaway: Crisis exposed an institutional gap.

moments.title: Federal Reserve Act
moments.body: Congress creates the Federal Reserve System with 12 regional banks and a central board.
moments.takeaway: Crisis-driven legislation built US central banking.

moments.title: Treasury-Fed Accord
moments.body: The Accord ends the Fed's wartime obligation to peg Treasury yields, restoring monetary policy independence.
moments.takeaway: Central-bank independence had to be won institutionally.

now.title: The Fed in modern crises
now.body: Fed responses to 2008 and 2020 redefined the scope of central-bank intervention.
now.open_questions: How accountable can independent central banks be in democracies?

items.reflection: The Federal Reserve's structure still reflects 1913 compromises between centralisation and regional autonomy.

moments.title: Maastricht Treaty
moments.body: Maastricht commits the EU to monetary union with convergence criteria for deficit, debt, inflation and exchange rates.
moments.takeaway: Monetary union was politically planned, economically uncertain.

moments.title: ECB founded
moments.body: The European Central Bank is established in Frankfurt with a primary inflation-targeting mandate.
moments.takeaway: Institutional design built on Bundesbank model.

moments.title: Euro launched
moments.body: The euro is launched on 1 January 1999, with notes and coins following in 2002.
moments.takeaway: Monetary union became operational.

now.title: ECB in crisis
now.body: ECB asset purchases and TLTROs reshape European monetary policy. The 'whatever it takes' commitment of 2012 redefined its role.
now.open_questions: Can the ECB conduct monetary policy across asymmetric economies in the long run?

items.reflection: The euro is the largest monetary union ever attempted between sovereign states.

moments.title: China joins WTO
moments.body: China's accession is the largest single integration event in globalisation history.
moments.takeaway: Trade liberalisation reshaped global manufacturing.

moments.title: China shock evidence
moments.body: Their paper documents the labour-market impact of Chinese import competition on US manufacturing regions.
moments.takeaway: Trade gains and losses were geographically concentrated.

moments.title: US-China tariff war
moments.body: Tariffs and counter-tariffs mark a partial retreat from the post-2001 trade order.
moments.takeaway: Trade politics reversed two decades of liberalisation.

now.title: Globalisation today
now.body: Friend-shoring, near-shoring and industrial policy reshape global value chains. Trade in services and digital continues to grow.
now.open_questions: What replaces hyper-globalisation as a governance framework?

items.reflection: China's WTO entry will likely be seen as the defining economic event of the early 21st century.

moments.title: Stern Review
moments.body: Stern argues climate change is the greatest market failure ever seen and that early action's benefits exceed costs.
moments.takeaway: Climate became a central economic problem.

moments.title: Discount rate debate
moments.body: Nordhaus criticises Stern's low discount rate as ethical rather than empirical, sparking ongoing debate.
moments.takeaway: Discounting future welfare is partly normative.

moments.title: Nordhaus Nobel Prize
moments.body: Nordhaus receives the Nobel for integrating climate change into long-run macroeconomic analysis.
moments.takeaway: Climate economics enters the canon.

now.title: Carbon pricing
now.body: EU ETS, UK ETS, and national carbon taxes implement integrated assessment model insights, while NGFS guides central bank climate analysis.
now.open_questions: How should integrated assessment models incorporate tail risks and tipping points?

items.reflection: Climate economics moved from niche to centre over two decades.

moments.title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century
moments.body: Piketty's book uses tax data from multiple countries to argue capital returns systematically exceed economic growth (r > g).
moments.takeaway: Long-run tax data revived classical inequality questions.

moments.title: Capital and Ideology
moments.body: Piketty extends the analysis to political ideologies justifying inequality across global history.
moments.takeaway: Ideology, not just economics, sustains inequality.

moments.title: World Inequality Report
moments.body: Coordinated cross-national inequality data become a standard reference for policy debate.
moments.takeaway: Open data infrastructure extends the research programme.

now.title: Wealth taxation debates
now.body: Piketty's wealth tax proposals have informed policy debates in France, the US (Warren) and EU.
now.open_questions: Are wealth taxes administratively feasible at scale?

items.reflection: Piketty's book sold over two million copies, unusual for a 700-page economics monograph.

moments.title: Capitalism and Freedom
moments.body: Friedman proposes a negative income tax to replace welfare bureaucracy with cash transfers.
moments.takeaway: Right-of-centre support for cash transfers has deeper roots than current debates suggest.

moments.title: Mincome experiment proposed
moments.body: US and Canadian negative income tax experiments run from the late 1960s to early 1970s, with mixed results on labour supply.
moments.takeaway: Income experiments produced ambiguous evidence.

moments.title: Finland basic income trial
moments.body: Finland's two-year basic income trial pays 560 euros monthly to 2,000 unemployed individuals.
moments.takeaway: Modern UBI trials are evaluated as RCTs.

now.title: Basic income debates
now.body: Sam Altman's OpenResearch UBI trial and a wave of pilots across cities and states keep UBI on policy agendas.
now.open_questions: Can UBI be financed sustainably without undermining work incentives?

items.reflection: Friedman and contemporary UBI advocates often share more than political surface suggests.

moments.title: Heckscher's foreign trade essay
moments.body: Heckscher argues countries export goods using their abundant factors intensively.
moments.takeaway: Trade reflects factor endowments.

moments.title: Ohlin's Interregional and International Trade
moments.body: Ohlin formalises and extends Heckscher's framework, founding the modern theory of trade.
moments.takeaway: Factor proportions became the standard trade model.

moments.title: Leontief paradox
moments.body: Leontief finds US exports are more labour-intensive than imports, contrary to Heckscher-Ohlin predictions, prompting decades of trade theory refinement.
moments.takeaway: Empirical paradoxes drive theoretical revision.

now.title: Trade theory now
now.body: Trade theory now integrates factor endowments, increasing returns, firm heterogeneity and global value chains.
now.open_questions: How does trade in tasks (services, data) fit Heckscher-Ohlin?

items.reflection: Swedish economists laid the foundations for a generation of US trade theory.

moments.title: John Maynard Keynes
moments.body: Minsky's book reinterprets Keynes through a financial-instability lens, distinguishing hedge, speculative and Ponzi finance.
moments.takeaway: Stability breeds instability in financial systems.

moments.title: Stabilizing an Unstable Economy
moments.body: Minsky's mature statement of financial instability hypothesis is largely ignored by mainstream economics.
moments.takeaway: Heterodox warnings can be ignored during boom times.

moments.title: Minsky moment
moments.body: The 2008 crisis revives Minsky's framework, with Paul McCulley coining 'Minsky moment'.
moments.takeaway: Crises rehabilitate previously marginal theorists.

now.title: Minsky in macroprudential policy
now.body: Minsky's framework informs macroprudential regulation, countercyclical buffers and stress testing.
now.open_questions: How can financial-instability frameworks be integrated into mainstream DSGE models?

items.reflection: Minsky's work was rediscovered when the world needed it most.

moments.title: Okun's Law
moments.body: Okun's paper establishes an empirical relationship between unemployment and output gaps in the US.
moments.takeaway: Empirical regularities became macroeconomic building blocks.

moments.title: Equality and Efficiency
moments.body: Okun's book frames the trade-off between equality and efficiency, with the famous 'leaky bucket' metaphor.
moments.takeaway: Trade-offs are made concrete by metaphor.

moments.title: Okun's death
moments.body: Okun dies suddenly at 51, leaving an unfinished theoretical framework that Brookings colleagues complete.
moments.takeaway: Even unfinished work can shape a discipline.

now.title: Okun's law today
now.body: Okun's coefficients have varied across countries and time, with COVID disruptions reopening empirical debate.
now.open_questions: Is Okun's law structurally stable under remote-work and AI displacement?

items.reflection: Okun was a macroeconomist who insisted theory match the data.

moments.title: Expectations and the Neutrality of Money
moments.body: Lucas applies rational expectations to monetary policy, finding anticipated policy ineffective.
moments.takeaway: Expectations changed how policy could be analysed.

moments.title: Lucas critique
moments.body: Lucas argues policy evaluation cannot use models whose parameters change with policy regimes.
moments.takeaway: Policy analysis requires deeper structural foundations.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Lucas receives the Nobel for the rational expectations hypothesis.
moments.takeaway: New classical economics reached the highest recognition.

now.title: New classical legacy
now.body: DSGE models grew out of new classical foundations. Post-2008 critiques highlight their limits in handling financial crises.
now.open_questions: Can rational expectations coexist with the empirical evidence of bounded rationality?

items.reflection: Lucas reshaped how macroeconomists thought policy analysis should be done.

moments.title: Production of Commodities by Means of Commodities
moments.body: Sraffa's slim book reconstructs classical political economy and triggers the Cambridge capital controversies.
moments.takeaway: Foundational critique can come in slim volumes.

moments.title: Reswitching demonstrated
moments.body: Cambridge UK economists show reswitching of techniques under varying interest rates, challenging neoclassical capital theory.
moments.takeaway: Aggregate capital cannot be straightforwardly measured.

moments.title: Samuelson concedes
moments.body: Samuelson concedes Cambridge UK's points in a 1966 QJE summary, but neoclassical practice largely continues unchanged.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical concession need not change practice.

now.title: Capital controversy today
now.body: Heterodox economists still draw on Sraffian frameworks; mainstream economics largely uses aggregate capital despite the criticisms.
now.open_questions: Do modern intangible-capital debates revive the Cambridge controversies?

items.reflection: Sraffa's work suggests the discipline's foundations are less secure than its practice assumes.

moments.title: The Nature of the Firm
moments.body: Coase asks why firms exist at all, given the market's coordinating role. Transaction costs explain the boundary.
moments.takeaway: Firms minimise transaction costs.

moments.title: The Problem of Social Cost
moments.body: Coase argues bargaining can resolve externalities absent transaction costs, reframing welfare economics.
moments.takeaway: Property rights and bargaining matter as much as Pigovian taxes.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Coase receives the Nobel for transaction costs and property rights analysis at 81.
moments.takeaway: A small number of influential papers can carry a career.

now.title: Coasean analysis online
now.body: Platform economics, blockchain governance and corporate boundaries analysis all draw on Coase.
now.open_questions: Do digital platforms lower transaction costs enough to dissolve firms or merely relocate them?

items.reflection: Coase wrote relatively few papers but reshaped multiple subfields.

moments.title: Owen takes over New Lanark
moments.body: Owen manages New Lanark cotton mills with shorter hours, infant schools and improved housing, while remaining profitable.
moments.takeaway: Welfare and profit could coexist in industrial management.

moments.title: New Harmony, Indiana
moments.body: Owen's utopian community in Indiana fails within three years but inspires the cooperative movement.
moments.takeaway: Utopian experiments often inform later reforms even when they fail.

moments.title: Rochdale Pioneers
moments.body: The Rochdale Equitable Pioneers Society codifies cooperative principles that spread globally.
moments.takeaway: Cooperative principles outlasted utopian projects.

now.title: Cooperative economy today
now.body: Cooperatives operate at scale in retail (Co-op, Mondragon), banking (credit unions) and platform cooperativism.
now.open_questions: Can platform cooperatives compete with venture-backed platforms?

items.reflection: Owen's mix of philanthropy, business and utopianism prefigured many contemporary social enterprise models.

moments.title: DICE model first published
moments.body: Nordhaus's Dynamic Integrated Climate-Economy model integrates climate and macroeconomic dynamics.
moments.takeaway: Climate-economy integration became computationally tractable.

moments.title: A Question of Balance
moments.body: Nordhaus updates the DICE framework and estimates optimal carbon-tax trajectories.
moments.takeaway: Optimal policy paths became part of climate debate.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Nordhaus shares the Nobel for integrating climate change into long-run macroeconomic analysis.
moments.takeaway: Climate economics enters the canon.

now.title: Integrated assessment debates
now.body: Nordhaus's framework is criticised for underweighting tail risks and using discount rates many find ethically inadequate.
now.open_questions: What models replace Nordhaus's framework if tipping points dominate?

items.reflection: Nordhaus's career embeds climate change in the standard macroeconomic toolkit.
